def: Having lost its nerve supply, so muscle becomes flaccid, atrophies and shows fibrillations and fasciculations.
Inability to identify an object by touch alone with intact basic sensation, from a lesion of the contralateral parietal cortex or dorsal column pathway.
A band of nerve fibers crossing the midline to connect the two halves of the brain or spinal cord, such as the anterior commissure.
A branch of the subclavian artery that supplies deep neck muscles and the upper intercostal spaces.
Present before pregnancy began, as in pregestational diabetes, which raises the risk of congenital malformations.
Relating to the junction of the pons and medulla in the brainstem, where cranial nerves VI to VIII emerge.
Located below the orbit. The infraorbital nerve is a branch of V2 supplying the cheek and upper lip.
A circular muscle around an opening. Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid (facial nerve); orbicularis oris purses the lips.
Having a normal number of cells, as in a bone marrow biopsy.
The main secretory cells of the pineal gland, producing melatonin.
Suppressing appetite, such as leptin and alpha-MSH signals from the hypothalamus.
Stimulating appetite, such as ghrelin and neuropeptide Y.
The thick posterior end of the corpus callosum connecting the occipital and parietal lobes of the two hemispheres.
A feeling of impending faint without complete loss of consciousness.
Crossing the tentorium cerebelli, as in herniation of the uncus through the tentorial notch, which compresses the oculomotor nerve.
The effect of a solution on cell volume, determined by its impermeable solutes. Isotonic solutions leave cells unchanged.
Relating to gastric pits (foveolae), the shallow depressions in stomach lining lined by mucus-secreting foveolar cells.
Relating to diverticula, outpouchings of the colon wall. Diverticular disease can cause bleeding or diverticulitis.
Located outside the lumen of a hollow organ, such as extraluminal air from a perforated bowel.
Next to the trachea; paratracheal lymph nodes are common sites of lung cancer and lymphoma spread.
Not containing bile. Nonbilious vomiting suggests an obstruction proximal to the ampulla, such as pyloric stenosis.
The connective tissue sheath around each muscle fiber. Inflammation of it is seen in polymyositis; antibodies to it occur in celiac disease.
Gas passing in the urine, suggesting a fistula between bladder and bowel or a gas-forming infection.
Reduced movement of the gastrointestinal tract, causing constipation or ileus.
Self-digestion of tissue by its own enzymes, as in acute pancreatitis.
Removal of the conjugate (such as glycine or taurine) from bile salts by intestinal bacteria.
Air in the biliary tree, seen after sphincterotomy or with gallstone ileus.
Relating to spondylosis, degenerative changes of the spine that can compress the cord or roots.
Relating to the pia and arachnoid, the inner meninges, as in leptomeningeal spread of cancer.
Laser treatment of the peripheral retina to destroy ischemic tissue, used in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
A white pupillary reflex instead of red, a sign of retinoblastoma, cataract or other retinal disease.
Occurring on waking, as hypnopompic hallucinations.
A subtype of depression with loss of pleasure, early-morning waking and weight loss.
Persistent inability to achieve orgasm, which can be caused by SSRIs.
Increased muscle tone, as in spasticity or rigidity.
Abnormal physical form, such as characteristic facial features in genetic syndromes.
Hallucinations occurring with preserved awareness, as in alcohol withdrawal.
An irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor given as eye drops for glaucoma.
A centrally acting muscle relaxant structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants, causing sedation and anticholinergic effects.
A histologic stain coloring collagen blue or green and muscle red. Used to show liver fibrosis.
The portion of the lesser omentum connecting the liver to the stomach.
Near the umbilicus. Paraumbilical veins link the portal and systemic circulations, forming caput medusae in portal hypertension.
Resembling basal cells, with small dark nuclei and scant cytoplasm.
A long strap-like thigh muscle that flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee. Supplied by the femoral nerve.
Behind the heart on a chest x-ray, as in left lower lobe collapse or hiatal hernia.
A pair of homologous chromosomes aligned together in prophase I of meiosis.
Derived from the middle embryonic germ layer, which forms muscle, bone, blood and kidney.
Causing narrowing or complete closure of a lumen, as in obliterative bronchiolitis.
Movement of leukocytes to the walls of blood vessels at the start of inflammation.
Escape of fluid or cells from a vessel into surrounding tissue.
Injected or applied within a lesion, such as intralesional steroids for keloids.
Relating to the junction between ribs and costal cartilage; costochondral junctions become beaded in rickets and scurvy.
Around a joint, as in periarticular osteopenia in rheumatoid arthritis.
Relating to the endomysium, the connective tissue around individual muscle fibers.
Death of muscle tissue, as in clostridial gas gangrene.
Muscle enlargement from fat and fibrous replacement rather than true muscle growth, as in the calves in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
